title: Fewshot contrapuntal probes — scratchbook
content:
Goal: lightweight personal log for building and stress-testing few-shot sets that intentionally pair contrasting examples (contrapuntal pairs) to surface collapse modes, hallucinations, and brittle instruction-following.

Why contrapuntal?
- Instead of clustering similar examples, put orthogonal/antagonistic exemplars adjacent so the model must discriminate intent and avoid overgeneralizing.
- Helps reveal: label bleed, instruction drift, priming collapse, and token-budget failure where earlier shots dominate.

Quick hypothesis list (to validate):
1) Contrapuntal pairs increase recall of minority intents but also raise class-confusion when examples share lexical overlap.
2) Short canonical examples (<= 20 tokens each) reduce primacy bias; longer narrative examples amplify drift.
3) Interleaving a 1-token separator token ("---") cuts KV cache leakage for some model variants.

Experiment notes (run 2025-02-15):
- Model: open-llm-xl-v2 @ hosted (test alias: open-xl-test-2025)
- Prompt template base: system instruction + 4-shot contrapuntal bank + query + response anchor
- Few-shot bank composition: 4 examples, arranged as A1 (intent X), B1 (intent Y, lexical overlap with X), A2 (variation X), B2 (variation Y).
- Temperature: 0.0 and 0.7 runs
- Observed: at T=0.0 sometimes returned the wrong 'style' (Y) when query aligned more subtly with X; at T=0.7 hallucination frequency increased ~12% compared to baseline clustered-shot bank.

Representative few-shot bank (raw) — minimal edits allowed for reproduction:
EXPLAIN: use the slot {QUERY} at the end.
---
Example 1 (A1)
Q: "Summarize the policy change for a legal summary."
A: "Short legal summary: The amendment clarifies employer notice obligations under Section 7; effective 60 days after publication."
---
Example 2 (B1)
Q: "Write a friendly newsletter blurb about a new product feature."
A: "Try this upbeat blurb: Our update makes exporting a breeze — try it today and see cleaner CSVs in seconds!"
---
Example 3 (A2)
Q: "Summarize the CFO guidance for internal finance team."
A: "TL;DR: focus on cash runway, trim discretionary spend, update forecasts biweekly."
---
Example 4 (B2)
Q: "Draft a casual social caption announcing a sale."
A: "Heads up — weekend sale! Save up to 30% on select items. Link in bio :)"
---
Query (slot)
Q: "{QUERY}"
A: (expected short, target 1-2 sentences)

Notes on failure cases observed:
- Label bleed: When the query includes neutral terms shared across legal and marketing (e.g., "policy", "update"), model sometimes outputs marketing tone despite legal shots included earlier.
- Overfitting to formatting: model rigidly copies sentence-start patterns from the closest previous shot (e.g., always starts with "Short legal summary:"). Solution idea: diversify lead tokens across examples.
- Token-saturation drift: longer examples (A2 length 30+ tokens) cause earlier A1 to be treated as less relevant. Consider reordering or truncating.

Quick mitigation experiments to try next: (TODOs)
- [ ] Swap order: B1, A1, B2, A2 and measure label accuracy delta.
- [ ] Insert explicit shot headers: "INTENT: legal" vs "INTENT: marketing" to test if explicit labels reduce confusion.
- [ ] Add micro-instructions between shots: one-line clarifications: "Example intent: legal-summary".
- [ ] Test with separator token variations: "---", "<|sep|>", "\n\n".
- [ ] Run same bank on quantized variants and Dedicated cluster (to check if kernel scheduling affects outputs).

Scoring rubric (quick, for low-effort eval runs):
- Intent match (0/1)
- Tone correctness (legal vs friendly vs casual) (0/1/2)
- Hallucination flag (0/1)
- Output length compliance (target 1-2 sentences) (0/1)
- Total (0-5)

Example failure capture (2025-02-15 14:08):
Input query: "Summarize the policy update about data export."
Model (observed): "Short legal summary: Our new export feature helps customers save and share CSVs faster."
Notes: blended legal 'summary' header with marketing content.
Score: Intent 0, Tone 0, Hallucination 1, Length 1 => total 2/5.

Ad-hoc hack ideas (brain dump):
- Use negative exemplars: include an explicit counterexample "Do not write as marketing blurb" with a short corrective shot.
- Use antonym priming: follow legal and marketing pair with a neutral anchor that says "Answer strictly in the style requested." Might reduce overgeneralization.
- Create a small few-shot toggle: preface query with single-shot 'style anchor' (one line) that the model must follow — test if that trumps earlier exemplars.

Logging conventions for reproducibility:
- Save full request and response, include model alias and commit SHA of prompt repo.
- Tag run with sample seed and temperature.
- Keep a tiny CSV of evals: timestamp, query, observed, score, notes.

Open questions / things to surface in sync with Maya/Ibrahim:
- Are we comfortable with including explicit 'INTENT' labels? Will it leak into production prompts as brittle?
- Should we add a post-filter step (light heuristic) to detect marketing language inside legal responses? If so, what's cheap: regex or embedding similarity?

Next steps (this week):
1) Implement order-swap AB test and gather 200 evals per condition (target: 2/15–2/21).
2) Try shot-headers vs negative-exemplar vs separator-only arms.
3) Push results (top 3 failure examples + summary) to JIRA-ENG-1327 and attach short CSV.
4) Demo quick playground in sync call (Wed) — bring examples that fail dramatically.

Random micro-notes to self:
- Keep at most 4 examples for quick productized prompts; >6 tends to increase latency and cognitive overload.
- When sharing with product, show 1 successful + 1 failure to illustrate tradeoffs.
- Save promising bank variants in prompt-bench repo under /contrapuntal-experiments/

End of scratchbook entry.

(If you re-find this in a month: search by tag "contrapuntal" or JIRA-ENG-1327.)
